questions.q: 'Walking is good exercise.' — gerund or participle, and why?
questions.a: Gerund — 'walking' is the subject, naming an activity as a thing. A wrong answer 'participle' shows shape-classification instead of job-classification.

questions.q: 'She wants to learn French.' — what is 'to learn' doing?
questions.a: Infinitive acting as the object of 'wants' — what she wants is to-learn-French. A wrong answer calling it a 'helping verb' misses that infinitives don't help, they name.

questions.q: 'The broken window frightened the children.' — what is 'broken'?
questions.a: Past participle used as an adjective describing 'window'. A wrong answer 'verb' misses that 'frightened' is the sentence's verb; 'broken' only describes.

questions.q: 'To err is human' — 'to err' is the subject, a thing, not an ______.

Fill in the blank: Non-finite verbs don't carry tense or agree with subjects — they are verb-forms doing other jobs: ______ (to go) act as nouns, gerunds (going) act as nouns, participles (going/gone) act as adjectives. 'To err is human' — 'to err' is the subject, a thing, not an action-in-time.

Fill in the blank: Same word, different job: 'Swimming is fun' — 'swimming' is the subject, a thing = gerund. 'The swimming champion smiled' — 'swimming' describes champion = ______. 'She loves to swim' — 'to swim' is what she loves = infinitive.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student identifies infinitive, gerund, and participle forms in sentences, names the job each is doing (noun vs adjective), and distinguishes gerunds from present participles.
